summary_html: Agency places a child with **relatives or kin caregivers** instead of non-relative foster care. Federal law favors kinship care as least-restrictive, family-preserving placement.

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Taryn M. v. State, Department of Family & Community Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: Denial of an ICWA-preferred relative's request for placement was affirmed because OCS proved by clear and convincing evidence that she was an unsuitable caretaker for a medically fragile child, although the superior court erred in assigning any burden to the relative.
key_cases.relevance: Sets the clear-and-convincing burden OCS must carry to reject an ICWA-preferred relative caregiver.
key_cases.quote: Because OCS demonstrated by clear and convincing evidence that the relative was an unsuitable caretaker, we affirm the superior court.

key_cases.case_name: In re Adoption of Sara J.
key_cases.holding: The prevailing social and cultural standards of the Indian community do not themselves govern the good-cause determination under ICWA § 1915, but remain relevant to the suitability of a preferred placement and may inform a special-needs good-cause finding; the good-cause findings here were affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: Defines the role tribal social and cultural standards play when the agency proposes to depart from the kinship and tribal placement preferences.
key_cases.quote: They may also inform, but need not control, any determination of whether a child's special needs or other circumstances constitute good cause to deviate from the preferences.

key_cases.case_name: Native Village of Tununak v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: Overruling its prior application of Adoption Rule 11's preponderance standard, the court held that good cause to deviate from ICWA's adoptive placement preferences must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, and vacated and remanded for application of that standard.
key_cases.relevance: Raises the State's burden when it proposes to bypass an extended-family or tribal placement.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that ICWA implicitly mandates that good cause to deviate from ICWA's adoptive placement preferences be proved by clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.case_name: Jacob v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: Grandparents were entitled to a declaratory judgment that OCS violated their statutory rights to notice of and participation in their grandchildren's CINA proceedings, but their remaining claims — including the request for systemic injunctive relief — became moot once they intervened.
key_cases.relevance: Confirms grandparents' statutory entitlement to notice and to be heard when placement of their grandchildren is decided.
key_cases.quote: We hold that all other issues are moot due to the Jacobs' subsequent intervention in their grandchildren's CINA proceedings.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court rejected every constitutional challenge to ICWA: Congress had Article I power to enact it, its placement and remedial-effort commands do not unconstitutionally commandeer state legislatures, courts or executive officers, and the equal-protection and nondelegation claims failed for want of standing.
key_cases.relevance: Confirms that the section 1915 placement preferences remain enforceable against state agencies, so Tununak, Sara J. and Taryn M. rest on a valid federal command.
key_cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners’ challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: ICWA section 1912(f) does not apply where the parent never had custody, section 1912(d) requires remedial efforts only where termination would precipitate the breakup of an existing Indian family, and section 1915(a) does not bar a non-Indian adoption when no other eligible candidate has sought to adopt; the South Carolina judgment was reversed.
key_cases.relevance: Limits the section 1915(a) preferences that Tununak and Sara J. enforce: they do not bar a non-preferred placement when no eligible preferred candidate has come forward.
key_cases.quote: Consistent with the statutory text, we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family’s “breakup” would be precipitated by the termination of the parent’s rights

common_failures: Failure to consider less restrictive alternatives
